why: Length carries no hazard of its own and predicts a wrong answer only because harder problems, where the base lacks the step, run longer, so its AUROC is modest rather than strong.
Long answers fail for lack of knowledge, not from drift, so a rule that acts on answers past 12,000 tokens resamples the same per-step skill and moves the 164 by only a few problems.
A per-step knowledge deficit gives systematic wrong answers on the problems the base cannot solve, so voting over 4 samples adds only a few problems to the single-sample 164.
With 115 of 328 problems wrong for both models and the base lacking the step on most RL-only ones, 4 samples recover only part of the 164-to-pass gap, landing near RL's 206.
The base has no length-driven drift for min-p to cure, and cutting the low-probability tail removes only a few per-step slips, so the score stays near the 410 at T 1.0.
Top-p 0.95 changes sampling of tail tokens but not per-step knowledge, and at T 1.0 the base does not degrade on its own text, so it scores like the 410 cell.
The base's long context carries no repetition attractor at T 1.0 (0 rule-A loops in 500), and mild min-p truncation at T 1.0 does not create one.
Cap hits are searches on problems the base cannot solve, a count set by knowledge, so min-p leaves them near the 27 of the T 1.0 cell.

RL's change shifts activations uniformly from the first token on, so a constant per-layer offset captures a large share of KL on the base's text, though less than the 69-86 % of copying all MLP weights.

The same position-independent offset applies on RL's own text, where whole-component copies close more KL than on base text (85.8 vs 69.4 % for all MLP), so the constant vector closes slightly more here.
The MLP carries most of the uniform shift (all-MLP 69.4 % vs attention 50.4 % on T1 text), so a constant MLP-output offset recovers about two thirds of the full constant-vector arm.
On RL text all-MLP closes 85.8 % against 69.4 % on base text, so the constant MLP-output offset closes proportionally more than on T1 text.
The base's 90 wrong answers come from missing knowledge that repeats across samples, so a 4-sample vote fixes only a handful over the single-sample 410.
Only 27 answers hit the cap at T 1.0 and they are problems the base does not know, so up to 2 restarts recover a few, about the 414 the T 0.6 restart row reached.
With the gap set by per-step knowledge, 4 samples reach only some of the 90 problems the base misses, leaving pass@4 below RL's single-sample 463.
